title: Minimum Path Sum
description:
Given an `m x n` grid of non-negative integers, find a path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell that **minimises the sum** of the numbers visited. You may move only right or down.

Return that minimum sum.
hints: Cells in the first row can only be reached from the left; cells in the first column only from above.
Any other cell is reached from above or from the left; its best cost is its own value plus the cheaper of those two.
Reuse one row of length n: when processing row i left to right, row[j] still holds the cost from the cell above and row[j-1] the new cost from the left.
approach:
**Key insight: because moves only go right or down, the cheapest way into a cell is its value plus the cheaper of the two cells that can lead into it.**

Let `dp[i][j]` be the minimum sum of a path from `(0,0)` to `(i,j)`. The first row and column are prefix sums (only one way in). For every other cell: `dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. The answer is `dp[m-1][n-1]`.

**Why it is correct:** the last step into `(i,j)` comes from above or from the left; the optimal path to `(i,j)` must use an optimal path to whichever of those it passes through (cutting and pasting a cheaper prefix would only reduce the total). Since the grid is a DAG under these moves, filling row by row processes every predecessor first.

**Space optimisation:** when sweeping row `i` left to right over a single array, `row[j]` still contains `dp[i-1][j]` (above) and `row[j-1]` already contains `dp[i][j-1]` (left), so `row[j] = grid[i][j] + min(row[j], row[j-1])` works in place. Modifying `grid` itself is another O(1)-extra-space option, but ask before destroying the input.

**Common mistakes:** initialising `row` to all zeros and then taking `min` with a fake 0 on the first row/column; treating the problem as a shortest path that allows moving up or left (then you need Dijkstra, not this DP).

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Allow all four directions (Dijkstra on the grid, `O(mn log(mn))`). (2) Return the actual path (walk backwards choosing the predecessor that produced the minimum). (3) Maximise instead of minimise, or count the number of minimum-sum paths (carry a second table).
